ruling.transaction: One BEGIN IMMEDIATE covering all three, which is the reworded must[0] read literally.
ruling.relationToP401: P4-01's append-only log stays the truth and is NOT part of the transaction: the JSONL append is the EFFECT of an outbox delivery, at-least-once, with the consumer idempotent on (messageId, epoch). The durable write is the transaction; the log is its projection.
ruling.turnCommitment: The inbox row's own state, so no new session event type is added. That is what keeps BLOCKED-088's case legal — goal-round-driver's deliberate restoration of a claimed message whose reservation went stale is a `released` row being re-claimed, not a forbidden transition out of a terminal state. ruling.classifyIntake: Stays a pure function. `seen` becomes the key set of rows in state `consumed`; the production call site is core/agent/src/inbox.ts's intake path, in the U stage.

openQuestions.question: Where does the private key live, and who may reach it?
options: kernel module-private WeakMap keyed by the signatureRoots handle, like P1-02's CONFIGURED_ANCHORS
a file backend under the dsh home
openQuestions.cost: The WeakMap keeps the key unreachable without the unforgeable handle and needs no filesystem policy, but the key then lives only for the process and cannot persist across restarts. A file backend persists and immediately raises mode, ownership and platform questions the delegate has already flagged (0600 for dev; production-controlled must REFUSE a file backend).
openQuestions.decidedBy: delegate — this is a durable-format and threat-model decision.

openQuestions.question: Per-install or per-process key generation?
options: generated once per install and persisted
openQuestions.cost: Per-process makes every restart invalidate outstanding tokens, which may be correct for a capability token whose lifetime is a session; per-install needs the persistence question answered first.

designPreFlight.notClaimed: Signing does not make the ROOT trustworthy. It makes a token's issuer checkable against a root this deployment configured. Whether that root is the right one is P1-02's question, and its answer is under P1-02's own lock — this epic must not borrow it. Recorded because 'tokens are now signed' reads as a stronger claim than it is.
designPreFlight.constraintHonoured: The user's standing rule that credentials belong only to them is untouched by this work: what P2-02 needs is code that MINTS a keypair inside the kernel at boot, never a key supplied to or held by the executor.

ruling.privateKey: Kernel module-private WeakMap keyed by the signatureRoots handle, the shape P1-02's CONFIGURED_ANCHORS already uses. The private key never leaves the kernel. The public key fills `signatureRoots`, which is the `Object.freeze({})` that made the marker bind nothing.
ruling.persistence: Through the credentials provider seam. Until P6-08's keychain lands, a 0600 file backend under the dsh home, with the profile marked `dev`; `production-controlled` REFUSES a file backend, fail-closed.
ruling.generation: Per INSTALL, minted at first boot — not per process, or every restart would invalidate outstanding tokens and P4-04's plan signatures. Rotatable: a new root plus the old public key retained for verification until expiry.
ruling.replacesMarker: `issueToken`/`attenuateToken`'s fixed marker and `verifyToken` comparing a candidate against that same marker is BLOCKED-135's shape a third time — a check equal to itself. Replaced by node:crypto Ed25519, following P1-02's `verifyPackageSignature` (null algorithm, since Ed25519 carries its own digest).
mustOneCases: after a non-root fiber is poisoned, verification still reaches the real kernel
a token still verifies after a restart
ruling.keyHandlingInTests: Every test mints its own keypair with `generateKeyPairSync` at run time; no key material is committed, and the executor holds no real private key. This is unchanged by the ruling and is recorded so the constraint is visible at the point someone would otherwise add a fixture key.

plannedCases.title: a token signed by the kernel verifies, and the SAME token with one byte changed does not
plannedCases.why: The positive control and the refusal together. Without the first, 'a forged token is refused' is satisfied by a verifier that refuses everything — which is what the marker path does in reverse today, accepting everything.

plannedCases.title: a token whose signature was produced by a DIFFERENT keypair is refused
plannedCases.why: Separates 'the bytes were tampered with' from 'the signer was not this kernel'. The marker cannot tell these apart because it is the same constant for every process.

plannedCases.title: an attenuated child token verifies against the same root, and a child claiming a capability its parent lacks does not
plannedCases.why: Attenuation may only narrow. Signing makes that checkable rather than declared: today a forged 'child' with widened capability carries the same marker as a real one.

plannedCases.title: after a non-root fiber's store is poisoned, verification still reaches the real kernel
plannedCases.why: SLICE-fiber-A closed the forgery; this pins that the token path specifically benefits, rather than assuming it inherits the fix.

plannedCases.title: a token issued before a restart still verifies after it
plannedCases.why: The per-install decision made observable. Per-process generation would fail exactly here, which is why the delegate ruled per-install.

plannedCases.title: `signatureRoots` carries the public key and NOT the private key
plannedCases.why: The handle is passed across the plugin boundary. A case that reads its members is the only thing standing between 'the private key lives in the kernel' and a refactor that quietly puts it on the handle.

adopted.name: node:sqlite / VACUUM INTO
adopted.reason: Adopted for the SQLITE BACKEND's implementation of the migration facet -- an atomically consistent copy of a live database without stopping its writers, which a file copy of a database being written to is not (the ledger row's `npm` is null because this is a Node built-in, not a package). Probed on this runtime rather than assumed: an in-memory database produced an 8192-byte copy. Its placement is the medium correction's whole point: it is one backend's snapshot primitive, not the transaction's medium. The transaction calls the facet; `storage-json` implements the same facet by copying a file or a directory tree, and no bundle mounts `storage-sqlite` today (base mounts `storage-json` at dshHomePath('storages')), so a sqlite-only design would have had no subject at all.

deviations.name: sequelize/umzug
deviations.reason: Not adopted: umzug runs an ORDERED LIST of migration scripts against a storage it owns, and records which ran. P1-10 needs neither half. The order comes from the manifest's declared DAG, which this epic validates for cycles and ambiguous edges before anything runs, and the record is the transaction's own two-phase intent/achievement file, whose split IS acceptance[1]'s property. Adopting it would put a second migration-state store beside the one the clause requires.

deviations.name: moxystudio/proper-lockfile
deviations.reason: Not adopted, and this was a real evaluation rather than a preference. The cross-process freeze this epic needs already ships: `@deepseek-ai/dsh-lease-sqlite` is mounted in bundle/base at dshHomePath('leases'), stores holder, epoch and expiry in a SQLite file, and issues FENCING tokens so a stale holder cannot write after being superseded -- which a mtime-and-pid lockfile cannot express. Adding proper-lockfile would put a second cross-process mutual-exclusion mechanism in a harness that already has one with strictly more semantics, and P4-07 already owns the refusal path (`held-by-another`, carrying the holder). The upgrade takes a run lease on a well-known work item before pnpm runs, and refuses the whole command when another process holds it.

makeVsUse.residual: The transaction itself: six phases over a storage facet, the manifest DAG decisions, and the reconciliation record. None of it is a library's -- what a library would bring is a migration RUNNER, and the runner is not the hard part. The hard part is that a crash at any phase must leave one whole version behind, which is a property of the ordering over this tree's own storage backends.
